statement: In people of European descent, mostly in UK Biobank, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more peripheral artery disease and possibly with abdominal aortic aneurysm and atrial fibrillation, while results for heart failure differ between the two genetic studies read, and no association was found with blood clots in the veins; the findings come from two studies whose outcome data overlap, some rest on few cases, and no absolute risks are given. Per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week (a unit the paper does not convert into drinks), the odds ratios were 3.05 (95% CI 1.92 to 4.85) for peripheral artery disease (3,415 cases), 2.55 (1.49 to 4.35) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; 2.60 (1.15 to 5.89) for abdominal aortic aneurysm (1,094 cases), 2.29 (0.89 to 5.93) after that allowance; 1.17 (1.00 to 1.37) for atrial fibrillation, 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32) after it; 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47) for heart failure; 1.04 (0.77 to 1.39) for venous thromboembolism; and 1.03 (0.56 to 1.90) for narrowing of the aortic valve, for which two other methods suggested a positive association and one indicated pleiotropy (Larsson et al., 2020). With the ADH1B variant alone, genetically higher intake was associated with peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with atrial fibrillation (1.24, 1.08 to 1.44; 14,367 cases) and heart failure (1.39, 1.08 to 1.78; 5,812 cases), the heart-failure result not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Two gene studies, both using a large UK study of volunteers, looked at other heart and blood-vessel problems. Genes for drinking more went with more narrowed arteries, mostly in the legs (peripheral artery disease), even after allowing for genes linked to smoking. In one study, links with a swollen main artery in the belly (aortic aneurysm) and with an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) became unclear once genes linked to smoking were allowed for; the other study found a link with an irregular heartbeat. For heart failure, the two studies disagreed. No link was found with blood clots in the veins. Some of these results rest on few cases, and neither study gave numbers out of 100.
population: People of European descent in genome-wide consortia (atrial fibrillation) and UK Biobank (the other outcomes) (Larsson et al.), and in UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.)
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake: up to 94 variants for log drinks a week, or the ADH1B rs1229984 variant alone (Larsson et al.); a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder (Biddinger et al.)
comparator: Lower genetically predicted intake (per standard deviation)
outcome: Peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, venous thromboembolism and aortic valve stenosis
magnitude: Larsson et al. 2020 (OR per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week; inverse-variance weighted, then adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation): peripheral artery disease 3.05 (1.92–4.85), 2.55 (1.49–4.35); abdominal aortic aneurysm 2.60 (1.15–5.89), 2.29 (0.89–5.93); atrial fibrillation 1.17 (1.00–1.37), 1.11 (0.93–1.32); heart failure 1.00 (0.68–1.47), 0.88 (0.57–1.37); venous thromboembolism 1.04 (0.77–1.39), 1.05 (0.75–1.47); aortic valve stenosis 1.03 (0.56–1.90), 0.94 (0.46–1.91), with pleiotropy indicated by MR-Egger; ADH1B variant alone positive (P < 0.05) for peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted consumption): atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08–1.44; P = .003), heart failure 1.39 (1.08–1.78; P = .009, threshold P < .008). No absolute risks.

With the ADH1B variant alone, genetically predicted drinking was associated (all P < 0.05) with higher odds of peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm, as well as stroke and coronary artery disease.

risk_of_bias.note: UK Biobank is in both the exposure and the outcome data of Larsson et al., which can bias estimates towards the conventional association; the instrument predicts smoking initiation, and allowing for it moved the aneurysm and atrial fibrillation estimates to no clear difference; pleiotropy was indicated for aortic valve stenosis; Biddinger et al. is rated high risk of bias overall (card sc_biddinger_2022) and its population for the disease analyses is unclear. The design protects against confounding by lifestyle, but the smoking-liability allowance shows the estimates can move materially, which is why risk of bias is rated down here although not for stroke.

inconsistency.note: Heart failure: 1.00 in one study, 1.39 in the other; atrial fibrillation borderline and attenuated in one, clearer in the other.

indirectness.note: European descent only; per SD of genetically predicted intake, not convertible into grams. Stated, not rated.

imprecision.note: Few cases for several outcomes (abdominal aortic aneurysm 1,094; aortic valve stenosis 2,244; peripheral artery disease 3,415) and wide intervals (aneurysm 1.15 to 5.89; valve 0.56 to 1.90).

large_effect.note: The peripheral artery disease ratio exceeds 2 but rests on one dataset with sample overlap and is per SD of an undefined unit; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief); rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Not independent: both studies use UK Biobank outcome data, and peripheral artery disease, aortic aneurysm, venous thromboembolism and aortic valve stenosis rest on UK Biobank alone in one study. Status mixed: the two studies differ for heart failure and partly for atrial fibrillation, and for the other outcomes only one study is available.
